title: The one who escaped
hook: Abd al-Rahman, an Umayyad prince, escapes to Spain and founds a new state

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fall: black banners from Khurasan, a hidden name spoken in Kufa, and the end of Umayyad rule in Damascus. Your line was: dynasties fall. How did you use the small power you hold? Day nine hundred twelve.

A young man is sitting in a house near the Euphrates when his small son runs in, frightened. Outside, black banners. The Abbasid horsemen have come for what is left of the Umayyad family. He grabs his younger brother and they run for the river. They plunge in and swim. From the bank, the soldiers shout: come back, you're safe, nobody will harm you. The younger brother, tired and afraid of drowning, turns back. The older one keeps swimming. From the far bank, the histories say, he watched them kill his brother. His name was Abd al-Rahman, a grandson of the caliph Hisham. Today: the one who escaped.
screen: `BLACK BANNERS OUTSIDE.` → `INTO THE EUPHRATES.` → `ONE TURNS BACK, ONE SWIMS ON.`

segments.voice: What do you do when everything you belonged to is gone? Abd al-Rahman went west. The Andalusian histories say he traveled in hiding through North Africa with a freedman named Badr, staying with his mother's people, the Berbers, for a time, slipping away when local rulers grew suspicious. Al-Andalus, across the strait, was full of quarreling factions, and among them were old clients and supporters of the Umayyad house. Badr crossed first to sound them out. Then Abd al-Rahman landed. He gathered supporters, defeated the governor, and entered Cordoba as its ruler. He didn't claim to be caliph. He ruled as emir, and the state he founded would last long after him. People gave him a nickname, al-Dakhil, the one who entered. And there's a tender story people tell. In a garden near Cordoba, he is said to have planted a palm tree, the kind that grew back in Syria, and written lines of poetry to it. In the poem, as the story goes, he speaks to the palm as a fellow stranger: you too are far from your home, you too were brought to a land not your own. So the founder of a state is remembered talking to a tree about homesickness. That's what makes this more than a war story. He lost much of his family, his city and his world. He did not get them back. He started again, in a new place, with what he carried.
screen: `WEST THROUGH NORTH AFRICA.` · `BADR CROSSES FIRST.` · `CORDOBA, AND AN EMIR.` · then, large: `A PALM FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: start again somewhere new. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Bring to mind a time something ended for you: a move, a loss, a door that closed. Breathe in. Notice what you carried out of it, even if it was small: a habit, a friend, a skill, a stubbornness. Breathe out. Now bring to mind one place in your life today where you could begin fresh. A new routine, a new conversation, a corner of the room. Choose one small first step you could take today. If you pray, you can ask for strength for new beginnings, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The one who escaped. Abd al-Rahman, the Umayyad prince who swam the Euphrates, crossed North Africa, and founded a new state in al-Andalus. Today's word.
Your line: he started again. Today, take the one small first step you chose, somewhere new. Day nine hundred twelve.

howItsDone: The story of Abd al-Rahman's escape and his palm-tree poem is retold in histories of al-Andalus, and the Great Mosque of Cordoba, which tradition says he began, still stands.

original.note: Arabic: the one who enters, the nickname given to Abd al-Rahman for entering al-Andalus.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who got lucky.
what it means: a refugee who lost his family and his world, and built a new state far away.
what a scholar hears: the Andalusian histories' escape story, the nickname al-Dakhil, and the palm-tree poem preserved in later anthologies.

sources.ref: Akhbar Majmu'a (Abd al-Rahman's escape across the Euphrates, his journey through North Africa, Badr, and his arrival in al-Andalus)
